excerpt: A 2017 Post and Courier analysis of 2011–2015 collision data recorded 629 crashes at the Ashley Phosphate Road and I-26 intersection in North Charleston — about one every three days, then the most of any intersection in the tri-county area and second in the state. In 2024 it still logged 174 collisions, second in the tri-county and fifth statewide (SCDPS). Here's why, and what your rights are if you're injured there.
keyTakeaways: A 2017 Post and Courier analysis of 2011–2015 collision data recorded 629 crashes at Ashley Phosphate Road and I-26 in North Charleston — about one every three days, more than at any other intersection in the tri-county area and second in the state behind I-20 at US-176 in Columbia. None of those 629 crashes was fatal, though 181 people were injured. In 2024 it recorded 174 collisions — second in Charleston County and the tri-county behind I-26 at US-78 and fifth statewide, with no deaths and 39 people injured (SCDPS 2024 Fact Book). Heavy volume — 170,500 vehicles a day on I-26 between Ashley Phosphate Road and Aviation Avenue (SCDOT, 2025) — and constant turning movements are the main contributors. Under S.C. Code § 15-3-530, injured victims have 3 years to file suit. Government entities like SCDOT may share liability for a malfunctioning or defective traffic signal they failed to fix after notice — but not for highway design — under the South Carolina Tort Claims Act, which has a two-year deadline (S.C. Code §§ 15-78-60(15), 15-78-110).

faqs.question: How often do crashes occur at Ashley Phosphate & I-26?
faqs.answer: A 2017 Post and Courier analysis of 2011–2015 collision data recorded 629 crashes at the Ashley Phosphate Road and I-26 intersection — roughly one every three days. That was more than at any other intersection in Berkeley, Charleston or Dorchester counties, and second in the state behind I-20 at US-176 in Columbia. Worth noting alongside the frequency: none of those 629 crashes was fatal, though 181 people were injured. In 2024, the latest state data, it recorded 174 collisions — about one every two days — second in Charleston County and the tri-county behind I-26 at US-78 and fifth statewide, with no deaths and 39 people injured (SCDPS).

faqs.question: What makes the Ashley Phosphate/I-26 intersection so dangerous?
faqs.answer: Several factors: vehicles leaving I-26 meet a signal shortly after exiting, left turns cross three lanes of opposing traffic, businesses along Ashley Phosphate Road create constant turning conflicts, and volume is heavy — 170,500 vehicles a day on I-26 between Ashley Phosphate Road and Aviation Avenue and 65,000 on Ashley Phosphate Road (SCDOT, 2025).

faqs.question: Who is responsible for crashes caused by dangerous intersection design?
faqs.answer: Under the South Carolina Tort Claims Act, SCDOT or another responsible agency may be liable when a traffic signal or sign was missing, defective or malfunctioning and was not fixed within a reasonable time after the agency knew or should have known — but agencies are not liable for the design of highways (S.C. Code § 15-78-60(15)). These claims have a shorter deadline — two years, or three if you choose to file a verified claim with the agency within one year (S.C. Code §§ 15-78-110, 15-78-80) — and damages are capped at $300,000 per person and $600,000 per occurrence (S.C. Code § 15-78-120), so contact an attorney promptly.

faqs.question: What should I do after an accident at Ashley Phosphate & I-26?
faqs.answer: Call 911 for a police report, seek immediate medical attention at Trident Medical Center, photograph the scene (including signal positions and vehicle locations), get witness contact information, do not give recorded statements to insurance companies, and contact a personal injury attorney who can preserve traffic camera footage and signal timing data before it is overwritten.
